# Results — Study 897 (CPPI Floor)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — **Constant-
Proportion Portfolio Insurance** (Black & Jones 1987; Perold & Sharpe 1988): hold a multiplier `m`
times the cushion (NAV minus a floor that accretes at the cash rate) in equities (SPY), the rest in
bills (BIL), rebalancing daily — a mechanical downside floor. Does the floor hold across 2008 / 2020
/ 2022, and what does the insurance cost in upside (excess-of-cash Sharpe) versus buy-and-hold?
Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. Data
as-of 2026-06-30 (the last complete calendar month; the partial current month is dropped).
Fingerprint `4b5a30d250b4` (SPY/IEF/BIL total-return prices).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily closes (`auto_adjust=True`, **total return**): SPY (risky leg), IEF (7–10y Tsy, a bond-safe-leg robustness), **BIL** (1–3m T-bills, the cash / floor-accretion / excess-of-cash proxy), **2007-05-31 → 2026-06-30**, 4,801 return rows |
| CPPI rule | `exposure_t = clip(m·(V−F), 0, lev_cap·V)` in SPY, remainder in BIL; **m = 5**, floor **F = 80%** of NAV **accreting at the cash rate**, `lev_cap = 1.0` (long-only); state read at the **previous close** (one lag, zero look-ahead), daily rebalance |
| Benchmarks | **buy-and-hold** 100% SPY (the upside the insurance is paid out of) and a **matched static mix** — a constant-mix book rebalanced daily to CPPI's realized average weight (isolates the *re-timing* question) |
| Fair race | all three books measured **excess-of-cash** (minus BIL); a constant fraction of SPY has the *same* excess-Sharpe as SPY, so the static and buy-and-hold Sharpes coincide and the honest re-timing read is the **spanning alpha** (CPPI on static, HAC *t* on the intercept) |
| Costs | one-way bps on the CPPI overlay's daily `\|Δw\|` turnover; a `band` tolerance available to brake whipsaw |
| Statistics | leverage/level-clean **spanning alpha**; a circular block-bootstrap CI on the excess-**Sharpe difference**; a HAC *t* on the daily excess-return difference; a two-era cut; a multiplier / floor / cost sweep; a **gap-risk** stress; a 30-seed synthetic control |

**Short history — named on the Signal axis.** BIL (the cash / floor-accretion leg) lists **2007-05-30**,
which bounds the joint window to ~19 years — one 19-year draw, not a law. It is a *favourable* draw for
an insurance rule, though: it **starts inside the GFC** and contains 2008, 2020 and 2022, exactly the
crashes a floor is built for.

## The race — CPPI vs buy-and-hold vs matched static mix (excess-of-cash, gross)

| book | excess Sharpe | CAGR | vol | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **CPPI** (m=5, floor 80%) | **0.164** | 2.37% | 7.94% | **−20.8%** |
| buy-and-hold SPY | **0.542** | 10.70% | 19.78% | **−55.2%** |
| matched static mix (avg w = 0.38) | 0.542 | 5.27% | 7.42% | −23.0% |

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| excess-Sharpe vs buy-and-hold | **−0.379** |
| excess-Sharpe vs matched static | −0.379 *(identical — see below)* |
| re-timing spanning alpha (CPPI on static) | **−1.56%/yr**, HAC ***t* = −1.16** (β = 0.705) |
| raw excess-diff HAC *t* | −2.15 |
| avg weight / overlay turnover | 0.38 / 2.3×/yr |
| floor breaches / min cushion | **0** / 0.0003 |

The mechanical floor **works**: max drawdown **−20.8%** versus buy-and-hold's **−55.2%**, and the floor
is **never breached** (SPY never fell > 20% in a single day, so the cushion never gapped through). But
that protection is bought **dollar-for-dollar out of the upside**: CPPI compounds at **2.37%/yr** versus
buy-and-hold's **10.70%**, and its **excess-of-cash Sharpe is 0.164 — a third of buy-and-hold's 0.542.**

**Why the static and buy-and-hold Sharpes are identical.** A *constant* fraction `w` of SPY funded from
cash earns `w · (SPY − cash)` in excess of cash — a pure rescaling that leaves the **excess-of-cash
Sharpe unchanged**. So holding CPPI's 38% average weight *statically* already matches buy-and-hold's
Sharpe (0.542); CPPI's only distinguishing act is the **dynamic re-timing**, and that **subtracts**
value here — a **−1.56%/yr spanning alpha** (the convexity/whipsaw cost was real, 2020 the poster
child).

## Bootstrap — circular block CI on the excess-Sharpe difference, CPPI − buy-and-hold (2,000 resamples)

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| Sharpe gain | **−0.379** |
| 95% CI | **[−0.691, −0.050]** |
| P(CPPI wins) | **1.4%** |

**The CI sits entirely below zero.** CPPI's Sharpe shortfall versus buy-and-hold is not sampling noise —
the insurance costs risk-adjusted return with ~99% confidence.

## Crash years — does the floor bite? (calendar-year total return & worst intra-year drawdown)

| year | buy-and-hold | CPPI |
|---|--:|--:|
| **2008** | −36.8% (DD −47.1%) | **−11.6% (DD −11.2%)** |
| **2020** | +18.3% (DD −33.7%) | **−4.8% (DD −16.3%)** |
| **2022** | −18.2% (DD −24.5%) | **−18.7% (DD −20.8%)** |

**2008 is CPPI's finest hour** — a −47% peak-to-trough cut to −11%. But **2020 is its worst nightmare**:
it de-risked into the fast February–March crash and was still in cash for the V-shaped snap-back, turning
buy-and-hold's **+18.3%** year into **−4.8%**. And **2022's slow grind was barely helped** (−18.7% vs
−18.2%): a floor tuned for a *crash* does little against a gentle, drawn-out bear that never trips the
cushion. Mechanical insurance protects against the crash it is shaped for — and whipsaws on the recovery.

## Robustness — two eras (split 2016-01-01)

| era | n | CPPI Sharpe | BH Sharpe | vs-BH | spanning α *t* | maxDD CPPI vs BH |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2007-05 → 2015-12 | 2,164 | **−0.464** | +0.335 | **−0.799** | **−2.38** | −17.5% vs −55.2% |
| 2016-01 → 2026-06 | 2,637 | +0.751 | +0.759 | −0.008 | −0.74 | −33.7% vs −33.7% |

The Sharpe shortfall is **concentrated in the volatile, GFC-and-2020-anchored first half** (the
re-timing alpha is *significantly negative*, *t* = −2.38); in the calmer 2016–2026 half CPPI roughly
**ties** buy-and-hold on Sharpe — but note the second-era maxDD is **the same as buy-and-hold's**: after
a long run-up the from-inception floor no longer sits under the elevated NAV, so the drawdown-from-peak
protection **fades** (a TIPP/ratchet floor would re-lock it — see references).

## Multiplier sweep — the protection/return frontier (gross); a 1-day drop > 1/m breaches the floor

| m | breach threshold | avg weight | CPPI Sharpe | maxDD | breaches |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 3 | 33% | 0.67 | +0.517 | −33.5% | 0 |
| 4 | 25% | 0.60 | +0.417 | −31.4% | 0 |
| **5** | **20%** | **0.38** | **+0.164** | **−20.8%** | **0** |
| 6 | 17% | 0.11 | −0.242 | −18.0% | 0 |
| 8 | 12% | 0.05 | −0.288 | −19.2% | 0 |

A clean **frontier, never a free lunch**: raising `m` deepens the de-risking (shallower drawdown) but
costs ever more Sharpe, and **no multiplier beats buy-and-hold's 0.542** — the closest, `m = 3`, gives up
almost all the protection (−33.5% drawdown). Higher `m` also lowers the breach threshold `1/m`: an
aggressive `m = 8` breaks the floor on any 1-day drop past **12.5%**.

## Floor robustness — a higher floor buys more protection at more upside give-up (m=5, gross)

| floor | CPPI Sharpe | maxDD | avg weight | CAGR |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 70% | +0.323 | −31.9% | 0.61 | 4.83% |
| 80% | +0.164 | −20.8% | 0.38 | 2.37% |
| 90% | +0.123 | −10.6% | 0.19 | 1.78% |

Same monotone trade-off from the other knob: a tighter floor caps the drawdown harder and drags the
return further. There is no setting where the floor is *free*.

## Costed — one-way bps on the CPPI overlay's daily turnover (m=5)

| one-way cost | CPPI Sharpe | BH Sharpe | vs-BH | maxDD (CPPI) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bp | 0.164 | 0.542 | −0.379 | −20.8% |
| 1 bp | 0.149 | 0.542 | −0.394 | −20.1% |
| 2 bp | 0.130 | 0.542 | −0.413 | −19.2% |
| 5 bp | 0.071 | 0.542 | −0.472 | −17.4% |
| 10 bp | −0.012 | 0.542 | −0.554 | −17.3% |

CPPI already **trails buy-and-hold at zero cost** — this is not a friction story, the return edge is
*absent gross*. Costs only widen the gap (turnover is a modest 2.3×/yr on the most liquid ETF alive, so
the insurance itself stays cheap; the drawdown cap survives every cost). There is no bankable *return*
edge to erode.

## Gap risk — the floor is a guarantee only between prices you can trade at

Splice a single overnight crash at the thinnest-cushion day (m=5 ⇒ breach threshold 1/m = **20%**):

| overnight gap | breaches floor? |
|---|:--:|
| 10% | no |
| 15% | no |
| **20%** | **yes** |
| 25% | yes |
| 30% | yes |

Daily rebalancing cannot pre-empt an overnight jump. At full exposure `w = m·C/V`, a one-day drop `d`
**breaks the floor iff `d > 1/m`**. In 2007–2026 SPY never gapped that far close-to-close (2008's worst
day ≈ −9%, 2020's ≈ −11%), so the real-tape floor held — but a **1987-style −20%+ open, a limit-down
gap, or a weekend event** would cut straight through it. The "insurance" carries un-hedged **gap risk**.

## Synthetic control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic seeded worlds (no network). The mechanical claim is a bounded drawdown, so the positive
control is a **bear** tape where the floor must visibly hold; the null is a **calm** tape with nothing to
protect; a **gap** knob checks the breach threshold.

| world | reads |
|---|--:|
| **bear** (drift < 0), **30 seeds** | drawdown protection mean **+0.520** (min +0.110), **floor breaches 0/30** ⇒ the floor holds mechanically |
| **calm** null (small positive drift, low vol), **30 seeds** | drawdown protection mean **+0.005** ⇒ nothing to protect |
| **gap 25%** (> 1/m = 20%), 20 seeds | floor breach fires in **20/20** |
| **gap 15%** (< 1/m = 20%), 20 seeds | floor breach fires in **0/20** |

The engine bounds the drawdown in a continuous fall, protects nothing when there is nothing to protect,
and breaches exactly when an overnight gap exceeds `1/m` — so the real-tape reads are genuine properties
of the SPY tape, not a broken engine.
*(A faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — MIXED.** Two claims travel under one name and they land oppositely. The **floor-protection
  claim is real and mechanical**: max drawdown **−20.8% vs buy-and-hold's −55.2%**, the floor **never
  breached** (0 breaches), 2008 cut from −47% to −11%, and a 30-seed synthetic control confirms the
  engine bounds the drawdown and never fires on a null. But the implied **"insurance improves the
  risk-adjusted outcome" claim is false**: CPPI's excess-of-cash Sharpe is **0.164 vs 0.542**
  (bootstrap gain −0.379, **95% CI [−0.691, −0.050]**, P(win) 1.4%), *no* multiplier or floor beats
  buy-and-hold, and the dynamic **re-timing subtracts** value (spanning α **−1.56%/yr**, *t* = −2.38 in
  the volatile era — 2020's de-risk-into-the-crash whipsaw is the archetype). A single-cycle,
  GFC-anchored, ~19-year BIL-bounded window. The floor is real; the free lunch is not.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** As a *return* edge there is nothing to bank — CPPI trails buy-and-hold on
  Sharpe and CAGR **gross, before a basis point of cost**, so friction is beside the point. The
  drawdown cap itself is cheap (2.3×/yr turnover on SPY, survives every cost) and genuinely bankable
  **as insurance** — but insurance is a *cost*, paid in full out of upside (2.4% CAGR vs 10.7%), not a
  paycheck, and it isn't even a hard guarantee: an overnight gap past 1/m = 20% breaches the floor. You
  run CPPI to reshape the payoff, not to earn — and the desk grades edges by whether they *earn*.
